parameter: NASA career space-radiation effective dose limit
context: Individual astronaut, total career, space flight radiation; universal for all ages and sexes

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, Revision B, requirement [V1 4030] (also in OCHMO-TB-020 Rev E technical brief)

quote: An individual astronaut's total career effective radiation dose due to space flight radiation exposure shall be less than 600 mSv. This limit is universal for all ages and sexes.
notes: Rev B approved 2022-01-05; Rev C approved 2023-09-15 and NASA's Oct 2023 LSAH newsletter still cites the 600 mSv career limit. Replaced the older age/sex-based limits. Technical brief: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/radiation-protection-technical-brief-ochmo.pdf

parameter: Typical ISS crew radiation dose rate
context: International Space Station, low Earth orbit

source.title: The Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health Newsletter, Oct 2023, Vol 28 Issue 2

quote: astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) receive doses in the order of 0.5 mSv/day
notes: Order-of-magnitude figure; varies with solar cycle, altitude, shielding and location. Same newsletter compares with Earth average background of about 2.4 mSv/year. Other NASA-affiliated sources quote 0.2-0.6 mSv/day (not fetched in full). NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev B rationale also uses ~0.5 mSv/day as the surface-mission reference environment.

parameter: Mars cruise galactic cosmic ray dose equivalent rate (Curiosity/MSL RAD)
context: Interplanetary cruise Earth to Mars inside MSL spacecraft (253-day transit), RAD instrument

source.title: Data From NASA Rover's Voyage to Mars Aids Planning (JPL news; science: Zeitlin et al. 2013, Science, 'Measurements of energetic particle radiation in transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory')

quote: an average of 1.8 milliSieverts of GCR per day on its journey to Mars
notes: Zeitlin et al. report 1.84 +/- 0.30 mSv/day (value seen in a Science paper table via search snippet; not read directly because science.org returned HTTP 403). The Science abstract (via Europe PMC) states the dose equivalent for the shortest round-trip transit 'is found to be 0.66 +/- 0.12 sievert'. Measured inside a shielded spacecraft during relatively quiet solar period; only ~5% from solar particles.

parameter: Mars surface galactic cosmic ray dose equivalent rate (Curiosity RAD)
context: Mars surface, Gale crater, ~300 sols 2012-2013 (solar maximum)

source.title: Mars' surface radiation environment measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity rover (Hassler et al., Science 343(6169), 2014); value as cited in arXiv:2208.00892 'Crewed Missions to Mars'

quote: According to Hassler et al. (2014) the average radiation dose at Gale Crater is 0.64 ± 0.12 mSv/day.
notes: Science paper itself was not retrievable (HTTP 403); the Europe PMC abstract confirms Hassler 2014 reports absorbed dose and dose equivalent from GCR and SEP but gives no per-day mSv. NASA Science page (https://science.nasa.gov/resource/radiation-measurements-on-mars/, 2013-12-09) gives the absorbed dose: 'a slowly varying dose rate of about 210 micrograys per day'. Quote's plus/minus sign appears as a replacement character because of PDF text extraction. Other sources round to ~0.67 mSv/day.

parameter: Lunar surface dose equivalent rate (Chang'e-4 LND)
context: Lunar surface, Von Karman crater (far side), Chang'e-4 lander, LND instrument

source.title: How intense and dangerous is cosmic radiation on the Moon? (DLR news on Zhang et al. 2020, Science Advances 6(39) eaaz1334)

quote: of around 60 microsieverts per hour
notes: About 1.4 mSv/day if continuous (60 x 24 = 1440 µSv/day; a Sci.News summary gives 1,369 µSv/day). DLR says the figure is the dose rate for a person in a spacesuit and ~200x higher than Earth's surface, 5-10x higher than a Frankfurt-New York flight. The primary paper's full text was not retrievable (science.org HTTP 403).

parameter: Lunar surface total absorbed dose rate in silicon (Chang'e-4 LND)
context: Lunar surface, Chang'e-4 lander, LND instrument; uncertainty +/- 1 µGy/h; neutral-particle component 3.1 +/- 0.5 µGy/h

source.title: First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface (Zhang et al., Science Advances 6(39), eaaz1334; PMID 32978156)

quote: We measured an average total absorbed dose rate in silicon of 13.2 ± 1 μGy/hour
notes: Absorbed dose (µGy) in silicon, not dose equivalent (µSv); do not mix with the 60 µSv/h dose-equivalent figure.

parameter: Artemis I (uncrewed Orion) total mission dose equivalent
context: Orion crew module interior, Artemis I, 25.5-day lunar flight, 16 Nov - 11 Dec 2022 (range across measurement locations/instruments)

source.title: Space radiation measurements during the Artemis I lunar mission (George et al., Nature 634, 48-52)

quote: Total mission dose equivalents were 26.7–35.4 mSv
notes: Of this, 1.80-3.94 mSv from Van Allen belt passes; GCR dose equivalent rates in Orion calculated at 0.96-1.24 mSv/day; cumulative absorbed dose up to 13.47 mGy. Uncrewed mission measurements (phantoms/detectors). NASA summary page (https://www.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/artemis-1/artemis-i-radiation-measurements-validate-orion-safety-for-astronauts/, 2024-10-09) gives no dose numbers.

parameter: Artemis II crew radiation dose (expected, pre-flight statement)
context: Crewed Orion lunar flyby, April 2026

source.title: To Protect Artemis II Astronauts, NASA Experts Keep Eyes on Sun

quote: comparable to a 1-month stay on the International Space Station
notes: No measured Artemis II mSv value found in NASA publications. Pre-flight NASA statement: expected exposure from radiation belts and GCR comparable to a 1-month ISS stay, about 5% of an astronaut's career limit (page updated 2026-03-17). Post-flight data to be released via NASA Life Sciences Data Archive (per a trade-press report; not verified at NASA). Quote is a fragment of the page's sentence.

parameter: Neutron share of total ISS radiation
context: International Space Station

source.title: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health

quote: Neutron radiation, which contributes to about 30% of total radiation on the ISS
notes: Approximate ('about'). Instruments per article: CANS (Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer), 'a compact and autonomous instrument designed to measure neutron radiation exposure in space' (CSA contract to Bubble Technology Industries, $5.5 million, for continued development); bubble detectors are described as a predecessor to CANS, used on the ISS by David Saint-Jacques. The article gives no dose values. Quotes are as relayed by the fetch tool's summarizer; re-read the page before final submission.

parameter: ISS/habitat cabin CO2 partial pressure limit (1-hour average)
context: Habitable volume, NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 [V2 6004]; ISS operates at or below 3 mmHg 24-h average since the 2016 flight rule

source.title: Carbon Dioxide (CO2) OCHMO-TB-004 Rev D, NASA-STD-3001 Medical Technical Brief

quote: The system shall limit the average 1-hour CO2 partial pressure (ppCO2) in the habitable volume to no more than 3 mmHg.
notes: Previously accepted range was 3.8 to 7.5 mmHg. Brief: limit keeps headache incidence below 1.4%; to keep headache risk below 1%, average 7-day CO2 should be below 2.5 mmHg. ISS levels have 'consistently remained at or below a 3.00 mmHg 24-hour average, with occasional higher brief excursions'; ISS historical range 1-9 mmHg. 0.5% CO2 = 3.8 mmHg.

parameter: CO2 level range associated with headaches
context: Anecdotal associations from spaceflight missions, ISS

source.title: Carbon Dioxide (CO2) OCHMO-TB-004 Rev D, NASA-STD-3001 Medical Technical Brief

quote: Headaches at levels between 2.8-4.5 mmHg; worsening with increasing levels of CO2 accompanied by fatigue and malaise flushing.
notes: Other NASA-listed symptoms: fatigue, malaise, decreased sleep and nausea above 4.5 mmHg; 5th cranial nerve dysesthesia at 4.5-5.0 mmHg; chronic cough, poor sleep, blurred vision and frontal headaches reported at 3.5 mmHg. Evidence is anecdotal.

parameter: ISS cabin total pressure (sea-level equivalent)
context: ISS cabin, typically 14.7 psia, 21% O2

source.title: Habitable Atmosphere OCHMO-TB-003 Rev A, NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief

quote: Currently, the ISS cabin pressure is typically maintained at 14.7 psia with 21% O2, which is equivalent to sea level.
notes: 101.3 kPa = 14.7 psia = 1 atm = 760 mmHg (conversion stated in the same brief). ISS oxygen fraction is 21%.

parameter: Allowed total cabin pressure range for indefinite crew exposure
context: Any crewed vehicle/habitat, NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D [V2 6006] (5.0 to 15.0 psia)

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Revision D

quote: The system shall maintain the pressure to which the crew is exposed to between 34.5 kPa < pressure ≤ 103 kPa (5 psia < pressure ≤ 15.0 psia) for indefinite human exposure
notes: Lower bound is exclusive (34.5 kPa < p). Quote taken from the standard's requirement as displayed in the technical briefs (OCHMO-TB-003/004); the Rev D PDF text confirms the 5 psia / 15 psia limits and the 30% diluent gas requirement [V2 6002].

parameter: Inspired oxygen partial pressure (PIO2) normoxia target range
context: Crewed vehicle/habitat, indefinite exposure, NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D Table 6.2-1 (2.80-3.00 psia)

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Revision D, Table 6.2-1 Inspired Oxygen Partial Pressure Exposure Ranges

quote: The system shall maintain inspired oxygen partial pressure (PIO2) in accordance with Table 6.2-1--Inspired Oxygen Partial Pressure Exposure Ranges.
notes: Table values (read from PDF text): Normoxia target PIO2 145-155 mmHg (indefinite); hyperoxia upper limit 356 mmHg (indefinite); mild hypoxia lower limit 127 mmHg (indefinite with monitoring). PIO2 is inspired (humidified) O2 pressure, not dry cabin ppO2. At sea level 14.7 psia / 21% O2 the dry-gas ppO2 is about 160 mmHg (21.3 kPa) by calculation (0.21 x 760), which is an inference, not a quoted NASA ISS value.

parameter: Crew health cabin temperature limits
context: Pressurized crew cabin, NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D [V2 6012] Crew Health Environmental Limits (excludes suited operations, ascent, entry, landing)

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Revision D, section 6.2.3.1

quote: Figure 6.2-2 is based on ASHRAE 55 and anchored at 18°C and 75% humidity on the upper left corner and 27 °C and 25% humidity on the lower right corner.
notes: Rationale text corner points of the Operating Limits figure (the figure itself is a graph, so limits are a temperature-humidity envelope, not independent box limits). Comfort/performance zone rationale cites studies supporting 20-25 °C and 30-60% humidity [V2 6013]. These are standard limits for design; actual ISS cabin setpoints were not fetched.

parameter: Crew health cabin relative humidity limits
context: Pressurized crew cabin, NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D [V2 6012] Crew Health Environmental Limits

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Revision D, section 6.2.3.1

quote: From an engineering perspective, average humidity is to be maintained above this lower limit (25%) to ensure that the environment is not too dry to prevent static electricity buildup within the cabin
notes: 75% is the upper-left anchor at 18 °C and 25% the lower-right anchor at 27 °C of the envelope; the envelope depends on temperature. Humidity outside limits can cause dry/irritated mucous membranes or skin rashes (microbial growth at high humidity).

parameter: One-way light time Earth to Moon
context: Average Earth-Moon distance (238,855 miles); Moon distance ranges ~357,000-407,000 km per NASA Moon Fact Sheet

source.title: Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day

quote: light can traverse that distance in 1.3 seconds
notes: Average value; min/max not stated by NASA in time units. Dividing the Moon Fact Sheet min/max distances (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html, updated 2024-01-11) by c gives roughly 1.2-1.36 s (calculation, not NASA-quoted). Round trip is about 2.6 s.

parameter: One-way light time Earth to Mars
context: Varies with orbital positions (closest approach to superior conjunction)

source.title: Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day

quote: it can take anywhere from three minutes to 22 minutes for light to travel between the two planets
notes: Consistent with NASA Mars Fact Sheet distances 54.6 to 401.4 million km (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html, updated 2025-05-19), which give about 3.0 to 22.3 min (calculation). An older NASA/JPL MGS FAQ gave about 4 to 21 min. Communications are also blacked out for ~2 weeks near solar conjunction.
